text: nevertheless. Online courses are convenient. Nevertheless, they cannot replace the energy of a live seminar.
furthermore. The program reduces costs. Furthermore, it improves student satisfaction.
consequently. The library extended its hours. Consequently, more students studied on campus.
moreover. The policy saves money. Moreover, it protects the most vulnerable students.
nonetheless. The sample was small. Nonetheless, the findings were consistent with earlier research.
conversely. Cities with more green space report happier residents. Conversely, crowded districts show higher stress levels.
accordingly. The deadline was moved. Accordingly, the team adjusted its schedule.
subsequently. The university introduced free tutoring, and subsequently its pass rate rose by 12 percent.
hence. The data were incomplete; hence the cautious conclusion.
thus. The survey was anonymous; thus, honest responses were more likely.
cohesion. Transition words give an essay cohesion, linking each paragraph to the next.
signpost. Phrases like 'firstly' and 'in contrast' act as signposts for the reader.
seamless. The lecturer delivered a seamless argument from introduction to conclusion.
chronological. A chronological structure works best when you describe a sequence of events.
transition. The essay lacks transitions, so the reader struggles to follow the argument.
coherence. A strong outline gives an essay coherence from start to finish.
unity. Each paragraph should have unity: one main idea, fully developed.
elaborate. The professor asked her to elaborate on her second point.
outline. She wrote a quick outline before her timed essay.
emphasis. The course places emphasis on critical thinking rather than memorization.
reinforce. Examples reinforce the main argument by making it concrete.
relevant. Only include details that are relevant to your main claim.
concise. Concise sentences are easier to follow than long, tangled ones.
redundant. 'Free gift' is redundant because a gift is always free.
digress. The essay digresses into personal stories and loses its focus.
framework. The T-S-C framework keeps each paragraph on track.
hierarchy. A clear hierarchy of ideas helps readers see what matters most.
overarching. The overarching goal of the course is independent thinking.
embed. Embed one short example inside each paragraph to support your claim.
streamline. The university streamlined its application process.
ambiguous. The instructions were ambiguous, so students interpreted them differently.
explicit. The rubric makes explicit what examiners expect in each paragraph.
implicit. The author makes an implicit assumption that all readers share her values.
nuanced. Her nuanced answer acknowledged both sides before choosing one.
subtle. There is a subtle difference between confidence and arrogance.
precise. Use precise numbers: '47 percent' is stronger than 'many'.
vague. A vague thesis ('technology is bad') cannot be supported well.
inherent. There are inherent risks in relying on a single source of data.
arbitrary. The deadline felt arbitrary rather than connected to real learning goals.
unequivocal. The evidence provides unequivocal support for the new policy.
distortion. Selective statistics create a distortion of the real situation.
connotation. 'Cheap' and 'affordable' share a meaning but differ in connotation.
oversimplify. It would oversimplify the debate to blame only social media.
perpetuate. Publishing only successful studies perpetuates a distorted picture of science.
depict. The chart depicts the rise in renewable energy use since 2010.
substantiate. The author fails to substantiate her claim with data.
refute. New evidence refutes the earlier assumption that class size does not matter.
concede. I concede that online courses are flexible, but they lack real interaction.
compelling. She presented a compelling case for stricter emissions rules.
outweigh. The benefits of early intervention clearly outweigh the costs.
valid. Both sides make valid points about remote work.
credible. The study is credible because it used a large, random sample.
warrant. The results warrant further investigation.
undermine. Small inconsistencies undermine the credibility of the whole argument.
bolster. Additional data would bolster the author's conclusion.
counterargument. Address one counterargument to show your view is balanced.
assertion. The essay is full of assertions but lacks supporting evidence.
premise. The argument rests on the premise that students learn best in silence.
bias. The survey suffers from bias because only volunteers responded.
plausible. Her explanation is plausible, but it needs more evidence.
mitigate. Planting trees can mitigate the effects of urban heat.
exacerbate. Cutting public transport would exacerbate traffic congestion.
foster. Group projects foster collaboration and communication skills.
hinder. Constant notifications hinder students' ability to focus.
alleviate. Flexible deadlines alleviate stress during exam season.
deteriorate. Air quality deteriorated sharply after the new factory opened.
catalyst. The pandemic acted as a catalyst for online education.
ramifications. The decision had serious ramifications for rural communities.
inevitable. Some job displacement is inevitable as automation spreads.
detrimental. Sleep deprivation is detrimental to academic performance.
profound. AI has had a profound impact on how research is conducted.
trigger. A single viral post can trigger a wave of misinformation.
curtail. Budget cuts curtailed the university's research programs.
escalate. Without intervention, the dispute escalated rapidly.
unprecedented. The move to remote work was unprecedented in scale.
derive. The findings derive from three years of fieldwork.
indicate. The results indicate a clear link between sleep and memory.
constitute. Women constitute over half of the university's graduates.
assess. The study assesses the impact of class size on achievement.
interpret. Critics interpret the data differently.
attribute. She attributes the improvement to better teaching, not more tests.
correlate. Income strongly correlates with access to higher education.
comprise. The sample comprises 500 students from five countries.
illustrate. The graph illustrates the decline in newspaper readership.
examine. The essay examines both sides of the debate.
evaluate. We must evaluate whether the benefits justify the costs.
infer. From the passage, we can infer that the author doubts the policy.
demonstrate. The experiment demonstrates that the method works under pressure.
hypothesise. Researchers hypothesise that the effect fades after six months.
verify. Always verify statistics before citing them.
allocate. Allocate two minutes for planning before you start writing.
prioritise. When time runs out, prioritise the longest writing task.
sustain. Chunk-writing helps you sustain momentum for ten minutes.
deadline. The deadline for the scholarship application is Friday.
procrastinate. Students who procrastinate often rely on last-minute panic.
efficient. A five-sentence frame makes your writing more efficient.
tedious. Copying notes by hand is tedious, but it aids memory.
meticulous. Meticulous proofreading catches the spelling errors examiners notice.
methodical. Adopting a methodical approach prevents panic in the final minutes.
feasible. A shorter, focused essay is more feasible than a perfect one.
sufficient. One example is not sufficient to prove a general claim.
anticipate. Good test-takers anticipate difficult questions and stay calm.
contingency. Have a contingency plan if the recording fails.
sequence. The paragraph follows a clear sequence: point, example, comment.
compress. You must compress two ideas into one sentence here.
comprehensive. The report offers a comprehensive review of the research.
deliberate. Deliberate practice, not repetition, improves writing.
strategic. Strategic use of transitions improves your writing score.
systematic. Keep a systematic record of your recurring errors.
proactive. Being proactive about deadlines prevents last-minute panic.
recurring. Spelling under pressure is a recurring issue in timed essays.
proficiency. Students can demonstrate proficiency through real projects.
threshold. A score above the threshold guarantees an interview.
exemplify. Her essay exemplifies how a short response can still be persuasive.
ensure. Proofread to ensure that no spelling errors remain.
psychology. The psychology of decision-making fascinates behavioural economists.
useful. Feedback is most useful when it is specific.
source. Always cite a reliable source for statistics.
research. The research suggests that feedback improves performance.
paramount. In academic writing, clarity is paramount.
